units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
That would be so, so sad, would it not?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: I am afraid, too, that Lord Illingworth regards woman simply as a toy. Now, I have never regarded woman as a toy. Woman is the intellectual helpmeet of man in public as in private life. Without her we should forget the true ideals.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: Sits down beside LADY STUTFIELD.
I am so very, very glad to hear you say that.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: You a married man, Mr. Kettle?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Kelvil, dear, Kelvil.
units.name: SIR JOHN

units.text: I am married, Lady Caroline.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: Family?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Yes.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: How many?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Eight.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: LADY STUTFIELD turns her attention to LORD ALFRED.
Mrs. Kettle and the children are, I suppose, at the seaside?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: SIR JOHN shrugs his shoulders .
My wife is at the seaside with the children, Lady Caroline.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: You will join them later on, no doubt?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: If my public engagements permit me.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: Your public life must be a great source of gratification to Mrs. Kettle.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Kelvil, my love, Kelvil.
units.name: SIR JOHN

units.text: To LORD ALFRED.
How very, very charming those gold-tipped cigarettes of yours are, Lord Alfred.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: They are awfully expensive. I can only afford them when I’m in debt.
units.name: LORD ALFRED

units.text: It must be terribly, terribly distressing to be in debt.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: One must have some occupation nowadays. If I hadn’t my debts I shouldn’t have anything to think about. All the chaps I know are in debt.
units.name: LORD ALFRED

units.text: But don’t the people to whom you owe the money give you a great, great deal of annoyance?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Enter Footman .
Oh, no, they write; I don’t.
units.name: LORD ALFRED

units.text: How very, very strange.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Ah, here is a letter, Caroline, from dear Mrs. Arbuthnot. She won’t dine. I am so sorry. But she will come in the evening. I am very pleased indeed. She is one of the sweetest of women. Writes a beautiful hand, too, so large, so firm.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Hands letter to LADY CAROLINE.
Looking at it .
A little lacking in femininity, Jane. Femininity is the quality I admire most in women.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Taking back letter and leaving it on table .
Oh! she is very feminine, Caroline, and so good too. You should hear what the Archdeacon says of her. He regards her as his right hand in the parish.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Footman speaks to her .
In the Yellow Drawing-room. Shall we all go in? Lady Stutfield, shall we go in to tea?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: With pleasure, Lady Hunstanton.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: They rise and proceed to go off .
SIR JOHN offers to carry LADY STUTFIELD’S cloak.
John! If you would allow your nephew to look after Lady Stutfield’s cloak, you might help me with my workbasket.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Enter LORD ILLINGWORTH and MRS. ALLONBY.
Certainly, my love.
units.name: SIR JOHN

units.text: Exeunt .
Curious thing, plain women are always jealous of their husbands, beautiful women never are!
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Beautiful women never have time. They are always so occupied in being jealous of other people’s husbands.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I should have thought Lady Caroline would have grown tired of conjugal anxiety by this time! Sir John is her fourth!
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY
